s_other.title: Test with a second device on the same Wi-Fi
s_other.text: Take a phone or another computer that is joined to the same Wi-Fi network. On a phone, switch mobile data off for this test, otherwise the phone quietly uses the cellular network. Open two websites you rarely visit, so nothing is shown from the cache.

s_captive.title: Look for the network's sign-in page
s_captive.text: Hotel, café, airport, train and guest networks often show 'connected' until you accept their terms on a sign-in page. Watch for a 'Sign in to network' notice, or open a new browser tab and type a simple address such as example.com – the sign-in page usually appears instead of the site.

s_toggle.title: Turn Wi-Fi off and on again (or restart the device)
s_toggle.text: Switch Wi-Fi off, wait about ten seconds and switch it on. The device rejoins and asks the router for a fresh address. A full restart does the same and also restarts stuck network software.

paths.win11: Quick settings (network icon on the taskbar) > Wi-Fi tile
paths.win10: Network icon on the taskbar > Wi-Fi button
paths.macold: Wi-Fi icon in the menu bar > Turn Wi-Fi Off, then On
paths.android: Settings > Network & internet > Internet > Wi-Fi switch (Samsung: Settings > Connections > Wi-Fi)

s_forget.title: Forget the network and join again
s_forget.text: Removing the saved network deletes its stored password and settings on this device. Joining again creates a clean profile. Have the Wi-Fi password ready first – it is often printed on the router's label as WPA key, Wireless key or Network key, unless someone changed it.

paths.win11: Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi > Manage known networks > (your network) > Forget
paths.win10: Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > Manage known networks > (your network) > Forget
paths.macnew: System Settings > Wi-Fi > Details… (or the … button) next to your network > Forget This Network
paths.macold: System Preferences > Network > Wi-Fi > Advanced > select the network > minus (–) button > OK > Apply
paths.ios: Settings > Wi-Fi > (i) next to your network > Forget This Network
paths.android: Settings > Network & internet > Internet > gear next to your network > Forget (Samsung: Settings > Connections > Wi-Fi > gear > Forget)

s_forget.undo: Pick the network from the Wi-Fi list again and enter its password – that restores the connection.

s_ipcheck.title: Check whether the device received an address
s_ipcheck.text: Every device needs an IP address from the router. A normal home address starts with 192.168., 10. or 172.16 to 172.31. An address starting with 169.254 – or none at all – means the device asked the router for an address and got no answer.

paths.win11: Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi > (your network) properties > IPv4 address
paths.win10: Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > (your network) > IPv4 address
paths.macnew: System Settings > Wi-Fi > Details… next to your network > TCP/IP
paths.macold: System Preferences > Network > Wi-Fi (IP address is shown under Status)
paths.ios: Settings > Wi-Fi > (i) next to your network > IP Address
paths.android: Settings > Network & internet > Internet > gear next to your network (IP address may be under Advanced)

cmds.what: Lists every network adapter with its IPv4 address and its Default Gateway (that is your router). Look in the block called 'Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi'.
cmds.not: It changes nothing and sends nothing over the internet.

cmds.what: Shows the IP address, subnet mask and router address that the Mac's Wi-Fi received.
cmds.not: It only reads settings; nothing is changed.

s_ping.title: Test the connection by number (no name lookup)
s_ping.text: This sends four tiny test packets to 1.1.1.1, a public server run by Cloudflare, using its number. If replies come back, the path through your router and provider works – and a failing website points to name lookup (DNS) or the browser.

cmds.what: Sends four echo requests and shows the reply time of each.
cmds.not: It does not test DNS. Some networks block ping, so 'Request timed out' alone is not proof that the internet is down.

cmds.what: Sends four echo requests and prints the reply time of each. Without -c 4 the Mac keeps pinging until you press Control-C.
cmds.not: It does not test DNS and changes no settings.

s_dnstest.title: Test name lookup (DNS)
s_dnstest.text: Websites are found by name. Your device asks a DNS server to turn a name like example.com into a number. If the number test works but this lookup fails, DNS is the broken part.

cmds.what: Asks the DNS server your device uses for the address of example.com. An 'Address' line under 'Name: example.com' means lookup works.
cmds.not: It does not change your DNS server or clear any cache.

cmds.what: Asks the DNS server for the address of example.com and prints the answer.
cmds.not: It changes nothing on the Mac.

s_flush.title: Clear the device's DNS cache
s_flush.text: The device remembers recent name lookups. A wrong or outdated entry can keep failing even after the network is fine again. Clearing the cache makes the device ask again.

cmds.what: Empties Windows' list of remembered name lookups. Windows answers 'Successfully flushed the DNS Resolver Cache'.
cmds.not: It does not change your DNS server, Wi-Fi settings or saved passwords.

cmds.what: Clears the Mac's DNS cache and tells the system's name service to reload. Terminal asks for your Mac login password; nothing is shown while you type it.
cmds.not: It does not change network settings or delete any files.

s_vpn.title: Switch off VPN, proxy or web filter for one test
s_vpn.text: A VPN app, a proxy setting or the 'web protection' of security software sits between your device and the internet. When it fails, every site fails while the Wi-Fi icon looks perfect. Pause it for one test – most VPN apps have a simple Disconnect button.

paths.win11: Settings > Network & internet > VPN, and Settings > Network & internet > Proxy
paths.win10: Settings > Network & Internet > VPN, and Settings > Network & Internet > Proxy
paths.macnew: System Settings > VPN, and System Settings > Wi-Fi > Details… > Proxies
paths.macold: System Preferences > Network (VPN services in the list) and Network > Wi-Fi > Advanced > Proxies
paths.ios: Settings > VPN (or Settings > General > VPN & Device Management)
paths.android: Settings > Network & internet > VPN (Samsung: Settings > Connections > More connection settings > VPN)

s_vpn.undo: Reconnect the VPN in its app, or switch the proxy back on. Before removing a manual proxy, write down its address and port so you can enter them again.

s_driver.title: Get the Wi-Fi driver only from Windows Update or the PC maker
s_driver.text: If this keeps happening on one Windows PC, an outdated Wi-Fi driver is a common cause. Install drivers only through Windows Update (optional updates) or from your PC or adapter manufacturer's official support website. Never use 'driver updater' tools or download sites.

paths.win11: Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates
paths.win10: Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update > View optional updates
paths.macnew: Not needed on a Mac – Wi-Fi drivers come with macOS updates (System Settings > General > Software Update)
paths.macold: Not needed on a Mac – Wi-Fi drivers come with macOS updates (System Preferences > Software Update)
paths.ios: Not needed – updates come with iOS/iPadOS (Settings > General > Software Update)
paths.android: Not needed – updates come with system updates (Settings > System > Software updates)

s_driver.undo: On Windows: Device Manager > Network adapters > your Wi-Fi adapter > Properties > Driver > Roll Back Driver (available when an older driver is kept).

s_netreset.title: Reset the network settings
s_netreset.text: This removes all saved Wi-Fi networks and their passwords, VPN connections and custom network settings, and reinstalls the network adapters. On Windows the PC restarts by itself after about five minutes – save open work first. Use it only after the other steps.

paths.win11: Settings > Network & internet > Advanced network settings > Network reset
paths.win10: Settings > Network & Internet > Status > Network reset
paths.macnew: There is no single reset button on a Mac: forget the network (System Settings > Wi-Fi) and restart the Mac
paths.macold: There is no single reset button on a Mac: forget the network (System Preferences > Network > Wi-Fi > Advanced) and restart
paths.ios: Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone (or iPad) > Reset > Reset Network Settings
paths.android: Settings > System > Reset options > Reset Wi-Fi, mobile & Bluetooth (Samsung: Settings > General management > Reset > Reset network settings)

s_netreset.undo: There is no undo. Afterwards you join your Wi-Fi again with its password and set up VPN apps again. Write down Wi-Fi passwords and any VPN or proxy details before you start.

s_lights.title: Read the router's status lights
s_lights.text: Most routers and modems have a light labeled Internet, WAN, Online, DSL or with a globe symbol. Steady usually means the line to the provider is up; off, red or blinking orange usually means it is not. The exact meaning is printed in the manual or on the maker's support site for your model.

s_restart_router.title: Restart modem and router in the right order
s_restart_router.text: Unplug the power of the router – and of the modem if it is a separate box. Wait 30 seconds. Plug in the modem first and wait until its lights settle, then the router. Give it two to five minutes before you test. Do not press the small recessed Reset button: that erases the router's settings, including the Wi-Fi password.

s_cable.title: Test with a network cable
s_cable.text: If a laptop or PC has an Ethernet port, connect it to one of the router's LAN ports with a cable and switch its Wi-Fi off. If the cable connection has internet, the provider and the router's internet side work and only the router's Wi-Fi is failing.

s_router_wifi.title: Check the router's Wi-Fi settings
s_router_wifi.text: Open the router's app or admin page (the address and login are usually on the router's label). Look for blocked devices, parental controls, access schedules or a guest network that is cut off from the internet. If the router came from your provider, its support can check it remotely.
s_router_wifi.undo: Change back only what you changed. Take a photo of each settings page before you edit it.

s_block.title: Check whether the router blocks this one device
s_block.text: Routers can refuse an address to a single device: through a device block list, a MAC address filter, parental controls or an access schedule. Phones and computers that use a private (random) Wi-Fi address look like a new device to the router and can fall under such a rule. Look for this device in the router's app or admin page.
s_block.undo: Remove only the block you found for this device, or switch the private Wi-Fi address back to how it was.

s_status.title: Check your provider for an outage
s_status.text: Use a phone on mobile data (Wi-Fi off) to open your internet provider's official status page, app or customer account. Type the provider's address yourself instead of tapping search ads.

s_provider.title: Contact your provider – with the fix log
s_provider.text: Use the contact details on your contract, your bill or the provider's official website – never a number from a search ad or a pop-up. Download or print the fix log on this page first: it shows that you have already restarted the router and tested several devices.

s_browser.title: Try a private window and a second browser
s_browser.text: Open a private (incognito) window, which starts without extensions and cookies, and try a second browser. If pages load there, the problem is an extension, the browser's own secure-DNS setting or its cache – not the network.

q_scope.q: Does everything fail on this device – or only one site or app?
q_scope.hint: Try three different websites in the browser plus an app such as email or a messenger.

answers.label: Only one site or app fails – others work

answers.label: Yes, it's a public or guest network
No, it's my home or office network

answers.label: Yes, after signing in it works
No sign-in page, or it still fails

q_others.q: Do other devices on the same Wi-Fi have internet right now?

answers.label: I have no other device to test

q_toggle.q: Switch Wi-Fi off and on (or restart the device). Is the internet back?

q_ip.q: Which IP address does the device have on this Wi-Fi?

answers.label: It starts with 169.254 – or there is none

q_forget.q: Forget the network and join it again with the password. Does it work now?

answers.label: No, still no address or no internet

q_ping.q: Does the number test (ping 1.1.1.1) get replies?

answers.label: I'm on a phone or tablet and can't run it

q_dns.q: Does the name test (nslookup example.com) return an address?

answers.label: No – it times out or the server fails

q_vpn.q: Is a VPN, proxy or security 'web protection' active? With it paused, does the internet work?

answers.label: No VPN or filter, or it still fails

q_lights.q: What does the router's Internet (WAN) light show?

answers.label: Normal – steady, as in the manual

q_restart.q: Restart modem and router in the right order. After five minutes, is the internet back?

q_cable.q: Does a computer connected to the router by cable have internet?

answers.label: No, the cable connection fails too
I have no cable or no port to test

q_status.q: Does your provider report an outage in your area?

answers.label: No outage reported, or I can't find out

r_onesite.title: Your internet works – the problem is that one site or app
r_onesite.text: When other sites and apps load, your device, Wi-Fi, router and provider are all doing their job. The fault is either the service itself or something between your browser and that one service.
r_onesite.why: Every layer below the service is proven by the sites that do load.

link.label: Continue with: one website won't load

r_captive.title: Solved: the network wanted you to sign in first
r_captive.text: Public and guest networks hold every connection until you accept their terms. Your device was connected to the Wi-Fi but the network let nothing through. If it happens again on the same network, open a new tab and the sign-in page should reappear.
r_captive.why: Internet worked immediately after the sign-in page – nothing on your device or at the provider had to change.

r_transient.title: Solved: a stuck connection on this device
r_transient.text: Reconnecting gave the device a fresh connection and address. A one-off is nothing to worry about. If it keeps coming back on the same Windows PC, update the Wi-Fi driver from the right source.
r_transient.why: Only this device was affected and a reconnect was enough – the router and provider were working all along.

r_profile.title: Solved: the saved network profile was the problem
r_profile.text: The device had stored settings for this network that no longer matched the router – for example after a router replacement, a new password or a changed security mode. Joining fresh created a clean profile.
r_profile.why: The same device worked as soon as it joined the network again from scratch.

r_noaddress.title: Likely here: this device doesn't get an address from the router
r_noaddress.text: The device joins the Wi-Fi but the router does not hand it an IP address. If other devices work, the router is probably refusing this one device, or the device's Wi-Fi adapter is not completing the connection.
r_noaddress.why: An address starting with 169.254 is what a device gives itself when no router answers its request.

r_dns.title: Likely here: name lookup (DNS) on this device
r_dns.text: Numbers get through, names don't. The connection works, but this device cannot turn website names into addresses – often an outdated cache, a VPN or filter that forces its own DNS, or a manually entered DNS server that no longer answers. The DNS guide on this site walks through changing DNS servers with an undo.
r_dns.why: ping 1.1.1.1 proved the route to the internet works; nslookup proved the name step fails.

r_browser.title: Likely here: the browser or an app on this device
r_browser.text: The connection works by number and by name, so the network is fine. When pages still don't load, the browser is usually the cause: an extension, a proxy setting, its own secure-DNS option or a damaged cache.
r_browser.why: Both the number test and the name test succeeded – the network layers below the browser work.

r_vpn.title: Likely here: the VPN, proxy or web filter
r_vpn.text: With the VPN, proxy or filter paused, the internet works. Update the app, choose another server location, or contact the VPN or security vendor. Turn the protection back on once it works again – don't leave it off just to save time.
r_vpn.why: Removing only that one piece of software brought the connection back.

r_device.title: Likely here: this device's network software or adapter
r_device.text: Other devices work, this one gets an address but cannot reach the internet, and no VPN is involved. The network settings or the Wi-Fi adapter of this one device are the remaining suspects. Work through the steps in order; the network reset is the last one.
r_device.why: The router hands out a valid address and other devices get through, so the fault is inside this device.

r_router_fixed.title: Solved: the router restart fixed it
r_router_fixed.text: Routers are small computers; after weeks of running, their software can hang while the lights still look normal. If you need to restart it more than about once a week, ask your provider about a firmware update or a replacement.
r_router_fixed.why: All devices failed together and came back together after the router restart.

r_router_wifi.title: Likely here: the router's Wi-Fi side
r_router_wifi.text: A cable connection works, so the provider and the router's internet connection are fine. The router's Wi-Fi is passing no traffic – often a guest network without internet access, parental controls, or a router that needs a firmware update.
r_router_wifi.why: The cable test bypasses Wi-Fi: it worked, so the line is up and the wireless part is the difference.

r_outage.title: Likely here: an outage at your provider
r_outage.text: Nothing on your side needs fixing. Don't reset the router or change settings while an outage is running – it won't help and can create a second problem. Check the status page again later and restart the router once the outage is declared over.
r_outage.why: All devices fail and the provider confirms a fault in your area.

r_line.title: Likely here: the connection between router and provider
r_line.text: All devices fail, the restart didn't help, and no cable test or outage notice cleared the router. Either the router has lost its connection to the provider, or the router itself has failed. The provider can check the line from their side – that is the next step.
r_line.why: Every device fails together, which rules out a single device; the remaining layers are the router and the provider's line.

q_toggle_s.q: Switch Wi-Fi off and on (or restart the device). Is the internet back?

q_ping_s.q: Does the number test (ping 1.1.1.1) get replies?

answers.label: I'm on a phone or tablet and can't run it

q_vpn_s.q: Is a VPN, proxy or security 'web protection' active? With it paused, does the internet work?

answers.label: No VPN or filter, or it still fails

q_restart_s.q: Restart modem and router in the right order. After five minutes, is the internet back?

r_router_solo.title: Solved: the router restart fixed it
r_router_solo.text: The router's software had probably hung. If you need to restart it often, ask your provider about a firmware update or a replacement.
r_router_solo.why: The internet came back right after the router restart, with no change on the device.

r_unclear.title: Not decided yet: this device or the router and provider
r_unclear.text: Without a second device, the checks can't tell whether the fault is on this device or behind it. A cable test, or any phone or computer borrowed for a minute, settles it. If other devices fail too, contact your provider with the fix log; if they work, the device-side steps on this page (reset network settings last) are next.
r_unclear.why: No VPN, no number test result and no second device – both sides of the router remain possible.
